newsitem.title: CHINA: China investors being pushed out of B shares.
newsitem.headline: China investors being pushed out of B shares.

text.p: Chinese securities authorities are determined to gradually force domestic investors out of the foreign currency B share markets to stop a leakage in foreign funds, analysts said on Monday.

The official media on Saturday confirmed rumours that swirled in the markets for weeks that the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges had banned mainland Chinese from buying new foreign currency B shares.

The two exchanges said that local investors must not buy any new B shares with immediate effect. They can sell B shares they hold and enjoy the rights of B share investors until they do. The exchanges did not set a deadline.

"The background to this is that not long ago, Shenzhen domestic investors poured money into the B share market there, and foreign funds took advantage of the situation to take profit and get out," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage.
"This goes completely against the original reason why the B share market was set up in the first place, and has resulted in a big outflow of foreign exchange," he added.
China set up the B share market in 1992 with the aim of allowing Chinese firms to raise money from overseas investors to fund their development.

The B share market in Shanghai closed slightly down on Monday but the Shenzhen B share index rose sharply despite the crackdown, with brokers saying the news had been completely digested ahead of the announcement on the basis of rumours.
Shanghai's B index closed down 0.58 percent at 40.059 points and its Shenzhen counterpart rose 2.24 percent to 89.32 points.
A Shanghai exchange offical said that investors with existing accounts must from now on prove their overseas nationality before they can buy new B shares.
"The new measure will be strictly implemented," he added.
A broker from Guotai Securities said trading in B shares by domestic investors over the past few months had made the foreign exchange market more confused.

"It has put pressure on the renminbi (Chinese yuan), especially in Shenzhen against the Hong Kong dollar," he said. "If it continues, it could cause a fall in the renminbi, which could affect the Hong Kong handover (from Britain in mid-1997)."

Brokers said the outlook for China's B share markets in the wake of the announcement was pessimistic, but added there was little risk of a wholesale sell-off because domestic investors couldn't buy and foreigners generally wanted out rather than in.
"Who are they going to sell to?" said Alex Conroy of ING Barings in Shanghai. "I don't see a lot of foreigners lining up to buy."
Domestic investors already holding B shares were also unlikely to want to sell at the current low levels, analysts said.
But the move has hurt market sentiment, and prices were expected to move lower in the near future, they added.
"The ban is a new blow to the B share markets, which have already been in depression for the past two years," said one stock analyst.

Other brokers said major domestic institutions such as Guotai and Shenyin & Wanguo Securities, which have been given special approval by the State Council to do B share business, were expected to support the makret.

"The institutions are likely to do some window-dressing business to support the market before the securities authorities can work out other ways to boost trading," said a second analyst. "This will prevent the markets from plunging."
